questions.question: What are the fields of a struct, and what types can they be?
questions.title: Struct Literal And Fields
questions.direct_answer: Named, typed slots — any type: builtins, other structs, pointers, slices, maps, channels, functions, interfaces, even the struct itself via pointer (for linked structures).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Struct Literal And Fields beyond memorized syntax.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving a definition without explaining a practical trade-off.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect the concept to a small production example and state its complexity or failure mode.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Named, typed slots — any type: builtins, other structs, pointers, slices, maps, channels, functions, interfaces, even the struct itself via pointer (for linked structures).

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A field is a named slot of a declared type inside the struct:

```go
type Node struct {
    Value    int          // builtin
    Children []*Node      // slice of pointers to THIS type — linked structures
    Meta     map[string]any
    Action   func() error // function field
    Clone    interface{} // interface field
}
```

Every type in the language is field-eligible: builtins, user structs (nested — and self-referential via pointer, which is how trees and lists exist: a struct cannot contain ITSELF by value (infinite size) but can contain a pointer to itself — fixed size), pointers, slices, maps, channels, functions, interfaces. The only layout rule: field types must be known sizes — which the pointer-to-self rule satisfies.

Zero values compose: a zero Node has Value 0, Children nil, Meta nil, Action nil, Clone nil — each field independently at ITS type's zero value. The struct is 'ready' with all fields zeroed — the zero-value design cascades into struct fields.

The promoted/exported rules: capitalized field names are exported (visible outside the package); lowercase are package-private. Unlike Go methods, there's no 'promoted field' mechanism beyond embedding's promotion — regular fields are accessed only through their name at the depth declared.

The layout fact interviewers probe: fields are laid out in DECLARATION ORDER (Go guarantees no reordering — unlike C compilers). The compiler may insert padding for alignment; you minimize it by ordering fields large-to-small. Two structs with identical field sets in different orders can have different sizes — and unsafe.Sizeof proves it.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The declaration-order guarantee is the deep one, because it's what Go REFUSES to do that C-family compilers do: no field reordering. The spec pins the layout: fields in written order, with implementation-defined padding. The result is (1) you can reason about memory use by reading the definition top-to-bottom — unsafe.Offsetof/Sizeof confirm the arithmetic; (2) struct types are interchangeable with C structs via cgo when layouts are written to match; (3) the size optimization is YOUR manual job — the govet fieldalignment check exists precisely to flag structs whose field order wastes padding (a struct with 1 bool, 1 int64, 1 bool uses 24 bytes: 8 (bool+pad) + 8 + 8; reordered int64-first-bools-last: 16 bytes — the optimization is real and mechanical).

Self-reference mechanics, one layer down: the compiler computes struct size bottom-up; a field of the SAME type by value would recurse infinitely — compile error 'invalid recursive type.' A pointer field is a fixed-size word whose pointee's size is irrelevant to the struct's own size — the recursion is broken by indirection. That's why every linked structure (lists, trees, graphs) in Go is built from pointers-to-self, and why the pattern type Node struct{ next *Node } is instantly recognizable as the shape.

The function-field distinction worth naming in interviews: a func FIELD (Action func() error) is data — assignable, nil-able, swappable per instance. A METHOD is on the type — fixed, promoted via embedding, part of the method set. The two compose the strategy pattern without interfaces when per-instance behavior is needed (each Node carries its own Action — set at construction, changed at runtime), while method sets handle per-TYPE behavior. Confusing them leads to 'I made a method but each instance needs a different one' — the field is the answer.

questions.question: What is the difference between exported and unexported struct fields?
questions.title: When would you use Struct Literal And Fields in a real project
questions.direct_answer: Capitalized names are exported — visible to other packages via the selector. Lowercase are unexported — package-private. This is THE visibility boundary in Go: one rule, applied to fields, methods, types, functions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Struct Literal And Fields.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Capitalized names are exported — visible to other packages via the selector. Lowercase are unexported — package-private. This is THE visibility boundary in Go: one rule, applied to fields, methods, types, functions.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Export is case, and case is the whole mechanism:

```go
package billing

type Invoice struct {
    ID    string  // exported: billing.Invoice.ID works anywhere
    total float64 // unexported: invisible outside billing
}
```

Outside the package, invoice.ID compiles; invoice.total does not — the selector on an unexported field is a compile error ('cannot refer to unexported field total').

The pattern this forces — and it's the architecture of half the standard library: unexported fields + exported accessors. time.Time is the exhibit: ALL fields unexported, all access through methods (Year(), Unix()...). Two reasons to do this, both structural:

1. Invariants: if total must never be negative (or must equal items-sum), exported access breaks any rule you can't enforce. Unexported + a SetTotal method that validates = the invariant lives in one place. Any exported field is a hole in the invariant's enforcement — no contract survives a direct write.

2. Freedom to change: unexported fields are implementation. You can rename, retype, restructure them without breaking any importer — the package's API (methods) is the only contract. An exported field is public API forever — changing its type is a breaking change.

What Go deliberately does NOT have: getter/setter syntax sugar (no properties), field visibility beyond the two levels (no protected, no internal-by-assembly). The result: the decision 'export or not' is the one visibility decision, made per identifier, and its consequences are total. The idiom that follows — exported struct = value object with plain fields (fmt's structs, config DTOs); unexported fields + methods = stateful object with invariants (time.Time, strings.Builder) — is the style guide written in case choices.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The mechanics of the selector rule: the compiler resolves x.total at the USE site's package. If the field's defining package differs and the name starts lowercase — undefined selector — a compile-time error, not a runtime hide. That's why 'unexported' means invisible, not inaccessible — the compiler simply has no path to the field from other packages (the symbol isn't in the package's export data).

The escape hatch people ask about and should know exists but rarely use: unsafe — unsafe.Pointer arithmetic can reach unexported fields (the implementation detail that gorm/encoding libraries sometimes leverage for performance). It's outside the type system's guarantees — 'unsafe' is the honest name — and any code doing it owns the breakage when layouts change.

The JSON interplay, because it's where the rule bites daily: encoding/json uses exported fields only. A struct with all-unexported fields serializes to {}. The workarounds — exported fields with json tags, or an exported DTO mirroring the domain struct, or MarshalJSON implemented manually — are the standard architectural choice points. The visibility rule and the serialization framework meet exactly here, and the 'domain struct + wire DTO' split is the clean answer when both needs are real.

The comparison that frames why Go's single rule is defensible: Java's four levels (public/protected/package/private) plus default-package semantics create a decision space per member; Go collapses it to one bit (uppercase or not). The cost: no 'visible to subpackage but not the world' — Go has no subpackage concept. The benefit: the visibility question is answerable by looking at ONE character of the name, and import cycles can't be partially broken by 'internal' visibility games. When teams need layered visibility, Go's answer is architecture (interfaces, small packages) — not finer-grained keywords.

questions.question: Can struct fields have default values or constructors?
questions.title: a common mistake when using Struct Literal And Fields
questions.direct_answer: No defaults — zero values ARE the defaults (every field at its type's zero). No constructors either — Go's answer is the zero value usable, plus ordinary functions (NewX()) when setup is genuinely needed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Struct Literal And Fields.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: No defaults — zero values ARE the defaults (every field at its type's zero). No constructors either — Go's answer is the zero value usable, plus ordinary functions (NewX()) when setup is genuinely needed.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The two absences and the design behind them:

No field defaults: a struct literal with missing fields gives those fields their ZERO values — not values you chose:

```go
type Server struct {
    Host string
    Port int
    TLS  bool
}

s := Server{Host: "api.example.com"}   // Port: 0, TLS: false
```

Port is 0 (the int zero) — not 8080 you might have wanted. There is no syntax anywhere for field defaults (no 'Port int = 8080' at the definition, no constructor magic filling it).

No constructors: no special method that runs at creation. What Go has instead is a three-layer convention:

1. Zero-value-usable design: for most types, the zero value works immediately (bytes.Buffer{}, sync.Mutex{}, strings.Builder{}). This is the preferred layer — the type is DESIGNED so zero is valid. When this is achievable, there's nothing to construct.

2. The New function: an ordinary exported function that returns a READY value:

```go
func NewServer(host string) *Server {
    return &Server{Host: host, Port: 8080, TLS: true}
}
```

Convention, not language — NewX() is recognizable, greppable, and takes arguments like any function. It returns either the value (Server) or, for pointer-receiver types, the pointer (*Server).

3. Validated construction (rare): when invariants must hold at creation, an unexported struct + New + methods — the caller can't build an invalid value.

The zero-value design pressure is the interesting part: it shapes types toward 'empty means empty-and-fine' (a Buffer's zero IS an empty buffer) rather than 'empty means broken' — and when a type genuinely can't have a valid zero (a Server with Port 0 might be invalid), THAT is the signal to reach for layer 2. Interviewers want the sequence: prefer zero-usable, else New, and the language gives you no third option — deliberately, so every type answers the question one of two ways, visibly.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why no constructors, mechanically: object construction in Go is just allocation + zeroing + (optionally) a literal's field writes — three things the language does directly. A constructor mechanism would add a hidden call at every literal/var creation — Go's cost model (every construct visible, no implicit execution) refuses it. The NewX convention keeps the call explicit: the reader SEES that a function runs and what its arguments are.

The zero-value-usability rule's deep rationale — from the language's own documentation: 'the zero value must be usable' is applied across the standard library as a design law, and its effect compounds: zero-value structs containing zero-value fields containing zero-value mutexes compose without any initialization chain. A global var x BigStruct with three embedded sync types is safe at program start — no init function, no order-of-initialization concerns. Constructors would reintroduce the initialization-order problem languages with static constructors fight.

The layer-2 nuance interviewers probe: NewX returning *Server versus Server. The rule follows the receiver convention: pointer-receiver methods on the type → the constructor returns the pointer (every use is *Server — uniform method set, see the interface batch). Value-receiver small types → return the value. The constructor choice is the FIRST place the receiver decision becomes visible to callers.

The anti-pattern to name: NewX that does real WORK (I/O, network) — a constructor that can fail should be (T, error), and one that does heavy work isn't a constructor, it's a function with a misleading name. Open/Load/Connect are honest names for that shape; New is for 'assembled a valid value' — the naming convention carries the failure semantics.

questions.question: What is an anonymous struct, and when would you use one?
questions.title: compare Struct Literal And Fields with an alternative
questions.direct_answer: A struct type defined inline in a variable or field declaration — no name, used once. Niche: one-off shapes — test fixtures, JSON envelopes, nested config — never a reusable type.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Struct Literal And Fields.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: A struct type defined inline in a variable or field declaration — no name, used once. Niche: one-off shapes — test fixtures, JSON envelopes, nested config — never a reusable type.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Deep Dive
sections.content:
The structural-identity mechanics: anonymous struct types are compared field-by-field (names, order, types, and tags — yes, tags participate in type identity). Two identical spellings in different functions denote the SAME type — assignment between them compiles. That's why the 'reuse by respelling' pattern type-checks: the language sees one type; the humans see two copies. The tension is the whole argument for naming at second use — the language won't force it, so discipline must.

The empty anonymous struct — struct{} — is a special case with real jobs: it occupies ZERO bytes (unsafe.Sizeof(struct{}{}) == 0), which is why it's the element type of sets (map[string]struct{} — the idiomatic set: no value storage, just keys) and the payload of done channels (chan struct{} — the channel exists for its close, carries no data; struct{} says so IN the type). A named struct{} would be ceremony; the anonymous one is a term of art.

The embedding corner: an anonymous struct can embed... a named struct (promotion applies — the fields arrive), or another anonymous struct. The JSON nesting patterns sometimes use this — envelope-in-envelope — and the same 'second use' rule applies with more force: two-level anonymous structures lose readers fast. The test: if a reader must count braces to know where they are, the shape needed a name an hour ago.

The standard library's calibration: anonymous structs appear in tests and marshaling glue throughout the stdlib's own test files, and almost never in exported API — the ecosystem's practice matches the rule exactly. Interviewers use this question to check whether a candidate knows the language supports it (not trivia) and has the judgment about where it belongs (the discriminator) — the answer above gives both.

questions.question: How do you access and modify struct fields — including nested ones?
questions.title: debug a problem involving Struct Literal And Fields
questions.direct_answer: Dot chains: user.Address.City. Pointer chains auto-dereference: p.Address.City (no -> in Go). Map fields need the value-copy-out pattern when mutating (non-addressable slots).

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Struct Literal And Fields.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Dot chains: user.Address.City. Pointer chains auto-dereference: p.Address.City (no -> in Go). Map fields need the value-copy-out pattern when mutating (non-addressable slots).

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The selector chain is the universal access form:

```go
type Address struct{ City, Zip string }
type User struct{ Name string; Address Address }

u := User{Address: Address{City: "Pune", Zip: "411"}}
u.Name = "Al"           // field
u.Address.City = "Mumbai" // nested — one chain

p := &u
p.Address.City = "Goa"   // pointer — auto-dereferenced, no p->Address
```

The pointer rule: Go has no -> operator — the dot works on pointers to structs directly (the compiler inserts the dereference). p.Address.City is (*p).Address.City. This eliminates an entire class of C/C++ syntax decisions and errors — chains are uniform whether the root is a value or a pointer.

The embedded-struct case composes the same way — promotion is field access at depth (admin.Name works because the lookup descends into the embedded User). Deep chains just get longer, not different.

The mutation exceptions — where dot-chains DON'T work for writing:

1. Map elements: m["a"].City = "x" — compile error (non-addressable — the map can move entries). The pattern: copy out, modify, store back (u := m["a"]; u.City = "x"; m["a"] = u) — or store *User values in the map so the mutation goes through the shared pointee.

2. Function returns and temporaries: same addressability rule — get the value into a variable first.

3. Value-receiver method chains: the method's copy is addressable but mutating it doesn't reach the caller — the earlier receiver batch's subject; the selector works, the write doesn't stick.

Reading is almost always fine — the exceptions are exclusively about WRITES needing stable addresses. The one-line summary: reads flow through any chain of values, pointers, and embedded structs; writes need every link addressable.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The auto-deref rule's mechanics: the selector p.Field compiles to a field access at a fixed offset from the pointer — the same code whether written (*p).Field or p.Field. The compiler knows p's static type (*User) and that . is a struct field selector — the combination means 'load field at offset.' No runtime dispatch, no nil check (a nil p with .Field panics — the nil-deref check is the hardware's, at the dereference). This is why struct field access is the fastest member access in the language — one memory load, statically computed offset.

The selector resolution order, formally, for chains: for a.Field, the compiler searches Field in the type's own fields (depth 0), then embedded types' fields (depth 1), then THEIR embedded (depth 2)... first hit wins; ties at the same depth are ambiguous (usable only via the full path — the embedding batch covered this). The chain u.Address.City is TWO selector resolutions (u → Address field; Address value → City field) — each statically computed. Nothing in the chain is dynamic — struct field access is compile-time-resolved layout arithmetic, every level.

The map-element mutation rule, mechanically, once more because it's the question's most common follow-up: m[k] on a map of struct values returns a COPY (the map stores values by value in its buckets; the lookup can't hand out a stable pointer because growth relocates buckets). m[k] = v compiles (copy IN); &m[k] doesn't (no stable address OUT). The workaround patterns reverse the indirection: map[string]*User stores pointer VALUES — m[k] returns a copy of the pointer (stable, one word), and .City through it writes the shared pointee. That's the canonical fix and the reason pointer-valued maps are the standard shape for mutable-struct collections.

The coda for interviews: 'no -> operator' is the surface observation; the depth is that Go unified value/pointer member access into one syntax with the compiler choosing (insert deref vs direct offset) from static types — which composes with the addressability rules to produce the write exceptions. The selector is simple BY DESIGN — all complexity moved into rules (addressability, method sets) that are checkable at compile time.
